beats.narration_text: 'Decides' is the word your brain reaches for — Claude picks the winning ledger. Wrong verb. gl-recon matches two ledgers, marks every disagreement, and stamps a likely cause on each gap. Deciding is the one thing it won't do. Here's why that choice matters.

beats.narration_text: Hear 'reconciliation skill' and it sounds like Claude has become an auditor — pulling up two ledgers and deciding which number is real. That's the natural read of the word 'reconcile'. It's also the wrong one.

Here's the giveaway: the skill never writes to either ledger. Run it on a period with a known break, and both numbers — GL and subledger — come out exactly as they went in. All that changes is a small object between them: a classified break. That's the design tell.

Here's the anchor. GL says one hundred four thousand for a position. Subledger says one hundred thousand. gl-recon lines up the two records, notes the four-thousand-dollar gap, and stamps a likely cause on it — call it a late trade. Nothing gets touched. The gap gets named.

The machinery is three steps in a fixed order: match, surface the break, classify the cause. Trade date or period, position or transaction level — the sequence never branches unless the SKILL.md itself says to. They optimized for reproducibility, not detective work.

production_viz.label: MATCH, SURFACE, CLASSIFY
production_viz.caption: in a fixed order, every run

beats.narration_text: So call it what it is — a matcher and a classifier, not a fixer. The payoff: run it twice on the same period, you get the same breaks tagged the same way. The trade-off: no opinion on which ledger is right. That call is still yours, by design.

Back to the anchor. gl-recon never picked a winner between the ledgers. It surfaced the four-thousand-dollar gap and tagged a likely cause. The number is still open — and that's the line the design draws on purpose.

Two honest limits, in both directions. A break tagged 'likely timing difference' isn't a promise the trade will settle and the gap will close — it's a hypothesis about cause, not a prediction of outcome. And a period that reconciles clean end to end isn't proof there's no error. It only means every difference in there happened to net to zero this run.
gl-recon doesn't decide which ledger is right — it matches GL to subledger, surfaces every break, and tags a likely cause; resolving the break is still on you.

Read the gl-recon skill and walk me through what you will do, before you do it. That way you see the exact fields it matches on before a single break gets classified. Go deeper: what happens when GL and subledger disagree at both position and transaction level, and which one does gl-recon use to classify the cause?
